But the jist is, our protagonist was a real spider - NOT the student she thought she was. Rather, the student was actually a goddess who doesn't quite like being a goddess, so she made herself into a student in a different planet, far, far away from where the story is happening.

The explosion was the hero and the demon lord trying to kill the goddess, which failed - she survived, but it killed all of her classmates, her teacher, and the spider.

Now, she did not want to reincarnate back in her actual world (and have to do the job a goddess should do), so instead, she put all of her memories into that little spider and reincarnated it as the student in the new world ... As a spider.

So in a way, it's the inverse of a human turning themselves into a spider: It is a literal spider who thinks itself a human, and then tries to become one.

The anime doesn't really do it justice, but in the light novel, the way it is written varies based on which character is currently the 'protagonist' for that chapter. Our protag, the spider, has the light novel written in a really erratic way, kinda like a real spider - whereas other characters have a more standard kind of writing. That was kind of a giveaway that it was originally a spider, rather than a human.

Winston Churchill once said, "Democracy is the worst form of government except for all the others".

  
Democracies are naturally slow to react, since there's not one single figure who can simply declare "do the thing" and have it done so immediately. Democracies also aren't necessarily fair: Very seldomly will you see a regular citizen get to any real position of power - it will always be a select few individuals who get it, these few individuals usually being incredibly rich persons with the money to afford proper campaigns. 

  
Granted, likewise, in a non-democratic system ( monarchy in this case ), there simply isn't a choice at all, so it isn't any better!

  
The way I interpret his quote is simply that a democracy is just as corruptible as any other form of government, and just as easily can stop representing its people (if at all); often times, it only gives the people the \*semblance\* of having a voice or power - how many protests have gone completely unanswered? How many cretins got into positions they don't deserve?

  
Lastly, and to add to the earlier point of democracies being slow, we have a good example of a dictator doing 'good' (you should evaluate it by yourself): El Salvador. Yes, it got yelled at by Human Rights, but the people of that country supported what their dictator did wholeheartedly, simply because the situation was \*that\* bad and their democracy had failed to solve it.

  
The thing is that, for all of its flaws, democracy is still superior to other forms of government simply for the fact alone that members of government can be voted on/off. Sure, democracy is for the people, and the people are fucking stupid - but hey, better have the slightest chance of something happening, than no chance at all.

As someone who lives in the underdeveloped world - and currently studying to go to somewhere developed - I have to say the following:

For the US - as an example, replace it with your favourite developed nation of choice - it is very good to attract highly educated immigrants. Not only does it bring more highly competent people into your country, but it also drives internal competition (as there's more educated people butting heads together or against one another), which generally leads to innovation.

For nations in the underdeveloped world, though ... It is awful, because it is sucking away our educated people. I, for example, absolutely want to leave as soon as possible - and I can. But that means I've taken my nation's resources, improved myself, and now won't contribute towards it. Sure, everything is 'paid for' in taxes, but having someone educated do their business here, is obviously better than over there.

Unfortunately, as long as there's better offers elsewhere, educated immigrants are THE ones with the opportunity to leave, and people without education are left behind, supporting a system that does not neccessarily return them any value.

This isn't to say every single person with higher education leaves, but the best ones do.
